utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Stewart, is the Defence ready to continue the cross-examination of Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar -- Madam Usher, would you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone, including you, Mr. Treanor. Important matters never become a routine, so therefore if I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony, this is not routine but an important matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As I indicated yesterday immediately before the adjournment, I wanted to come on to the question of the six strategic goals, as they are often called, which you had -- for the reference, you had dealt with in your evidence before this Court. The beginning point is 17/09 or 17/10 of the transcript, where you went through those goals.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There are a couple of documents which it would be, I think, quite helpful for everybody to have reasonably to hand. They are in -- the main ones are in file or bundle 12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I brought the next four. It would certainly have been helpful if I would have been aware that it was the twelfth binder that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, I'm so sorry, Your Honour. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, no, we'll solve -- we'll solve the problem anyhow. But just to remind you that whenever you move even more quickly than expected, to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, absolutely, Your Honour. It's entirely my fault. I should have seen that we'd race on through the bundles.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the meantime, we have an extra copy here, if it would be of assistance to the Court, of that particular binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's start. I'll have a copy soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The two particular items which it is helpful for everybody to have to hand or in mind are the minutes or record of the 12th of May, 1992 Assembly of the -- it's the 16th session of the Assembly of the Serbian People, the 12th of May, 1992, and that's at tab 127, and in particular at page 13 of the English version of that document we have Mr. Karadzic going through the six goals. And that's at the B/C/S version pages 7 and 8. The first point is this, sir, Mr. Treanor: The Sixteenth Assembly, which is one that I've just mentioned where these strategic objectives or strategic goals were discussed, that was on the 12th of May, 1992, that was the first Assembly, Serb Assembly after the outbreak of war, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the first session since the -- it was the 6th of April, on which day the -- or late in the evening the Fifteenth Session was held. It's basically the outbreak of the war --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I understand, Mr. Treanor. So you're saying that the precise definition of the outbreak of war is a matter of some debate. That's really what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right. Well, anyway, we needn't get into it, because there was that previous session, and this was -- and this particular -- so that earlier session came, one might say, right in the middle of the period when everybody would accept that sometime, broadly, war broke out.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm not entering into, I should say, technical definitions of "war," legal definitions of "war," states of war, as opposed to imminent states of war, and so on. I'm talking about what you might call real-life war, fighting that broke out in a serious manner. I should just clarify that. So far as you've been able to see -- well, the background was that the -- on the 7th of April the independence of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina had been proclaimed or declared by the Serbs, hadn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it was the evening of the 6th of April to the 7th of April, in a late-night session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And the European Union - or perhaps it was the European Community at the time, I don't know - had suspended negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure precisely what the technicalities were, but negotiations were not ongoing at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. The European Community was not prepared to continue negotiations while this extreme state of hostility continued.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what their position was on that issue at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's fair. The -- from your reading of the materials that you have seen, is it fair to say that at least a number of the deputies in the Serb Assembly were in a fairly warlike frame of mind?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: When?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At the 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, at that session.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Among other things, they had, apart from simply the fighting, they had heard reports of atrocities against Serbs, hadn't they?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't recall whether that's reflected in the record of the session. It may be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As always, if you don't know, that's an entirely fair answer. If you don't know, that's just what I invite you to say. That's the position you --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You don't know on that. Okay. And they also -- can you say whether it's apparent that a number of the deputies also felt that they, the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, had in some sense been thrown out of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall that that was expressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been, and I have read the whole session. It's rather lengthy, and I can't recall that having come out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would you accept from everything you've seen and your reading that at this particular point, 12th of May, when they held the Sixteenth Session of the Serb Assembly it would have been at the very least politically very difficult, verging on the impossible, for the Serb leadership to present to the deputies in the Serb Assembly and argue for the Cutilheiro Plan in terms?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the -- I don't know. After all, the Cutilheiro Plan was not really a plan. It was a framework for negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you say whether your impression from the material you've looked at is that the Serb leadership at that time - and I'm still talking about 12th of May, 1992 - despite the extreme hostilities, apparently wanted to continue the international -- internationally sponsored negotiations if at all possible?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that certainly prior to that they -- Dr. Karadzic had issued a platform relating to the continuance of negotiations. So I think it's fair to say that he would have been in favour of continuing those negotiations under certain conditions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is the -- is the position that, as at 12th of May, 1992, Dr. Karadzic in particular was faced with the type of difficulty that we've considered before, which was that he -- if he were at some point to continue with these internationally sponsored negotiations he had to sell that to the Serb Assembly?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at some point he -- he would -- he would have.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And at that point, it wouldn't be -- I mean, it wasn't an easy selling job.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not clear to me that that's what he was doing on May the 12th. I don't think that was imminent at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could you go - because I think it's helpful if we all refresh our minds, and it's fair to you, Mr. Treanor - could you go to tab 127 in Volume 12. And we've got the minutes of the Sixteenth Session that I referred to, chaired, not surprisingly, by Mr. Krajisnik, as the President of the Assembly, and this is - and we've looked at it already - but this is the meeting, and it's recorded in the minutes at which the six strategic goals were discussed in some detail, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: They're not -- they're not identified as a separate item on the agenda, in the first place, are they?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, in fact, they weren't the subject of a separate specific decision either, were they? Identified as such in the minutes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a good point. The goals as set forth in the record of the session are part of the report that Dr. Karadzic delivers, which is an agenda item, I think. I think it's -- it would be the first agenda item.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And at the end of that report, the Assembly adopts or approves the report. That is the only record of the goals being adopted in the record of the session, as far as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Treanor, I should make it clear it's not my case that the goals were not adopted and approved by this meeting, because they plainly were in exactly the way you describe. They formed part of Dr. Karadzic's report under item 1, and the report was adopted and approved, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The six strategic objectives - I think somebody has called them goals in the past, but everybody knows what I'm talking about if I use "goals"; anyway, it's shorter - they were published, we know, in the Official Gazette, and that's at tab 130, dated at the bottom -- we've been over this ground -- dated at the bottom the 12th of May, because that's the date of the -- of the decision as part of the broader adoption of the report by the Assembly, the actual publication being a considerable time later, apparently the 26th of November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's right, isn't it? The -- it might be helpful, if it's not inconvenient to you, Mr. Treanor and others, it might be helpful, since it is a single page, if you -- it's up to you, but if you wanted to take it out and just have it on one side, because I'm going to invite some comparison between what was said in the minutes of the session of the 12th of May and what appears in the Official Gazette. So rather than having you jumping backwards and forwards from one tab to the other, that single sheet can easily come out. The discussion of these goals -- actually, "goals" is the word that is used in the English translation of the minutes, and that's where I got it from. The discussion is at page 13 of the English. It starts at page 7, and goes on to page 8 of the B/C/S version. And we have about -- you highlighted these in your evidence before. Just before halfway down, the paragraph beginning "The Serbian side in Bosnia and Herzegovina." You have that, Mr. Treanor, do you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you going to -- may I ask, are you going to work from the English on this or from the B/C/S, or both?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- I would say both. It depends on what you're going to be asking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm simply going to be asking you questions from the English, because I'm afraid that's all I can do. I just wanted to be clear. You, of course, Mr. Treanor, you're entirely free. It's the documents you put in and you have both versions.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, refresh my memory. It was on pages ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It should be on page 7. I was looking at it. It should start at page 7 of the B/C/S version, possibly page 8.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- so we start off -- and this is Dr. Karadzic talking. He's introduced this by saying "It would be best if a truce could be established." That's the passage immediately above. "It would be best if a truce could be established right away and borders set up, even if we were to lose something in the manner of the European Community proposes and agrees with the three national communities." And then he continues: "The Serbian side in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Presidency, the government, the Council for National Security which we have set up have formulated these strategic priorities, that is to say, the strategic goals for the Serbian people. The first such goal is separation from the other two national communities and separation of states." My first question here for you, Mr. Treanor, is: Looking at the way that Dr. Karadzic expresses it there in the minutes - and I'm sure that you're going to find it helpful to look at the B/C/S version for this - but may I also -- I did suggest you took out 130, the Official Gazette publication, but I expect it was the English version that was taken out, but I would invite --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the original as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've got the original. I was going to say, I invite you to do it, because this is the comparison. Can you say whether in your view there is any discrepancy between the way in which Dr. Karadzic expresses the first goal and the way in which it is expressed in the publication in the Official Gazette?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, the words are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay. So -- so discrepancy in the sense of the wording being different. So beyond that, then, is there any discrepancy, in your view, as far as the meaning is concerned?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are two differences. In the published version, the formulation is shorter, and it's not a full sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic's speech here contains a complete sentence: "The first goal," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. So let's ignore the first such goal, because in a sense that's the equivalent of the number 1, isn't is, in the Official Gazette. So we can put that to one side.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In addition, the word for "separation" as is used in the translation of the Assembly record is razdvajanje, which means to sort of put in two. The root there is the word "two." In the Gazette item, the comparable word which seems to have been rendered in the English translation of the Gazette version, if I can describe it that way, has been rendered as "establishing borders; separating." And the root of the Serbian word is razgranicenje, the root of that word being granice, which means border or frontier. So the idea -- the root idea of that word is the forming of borders, as opposed to dividing in two.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I wonder if I might just pause there, Your Honour, and invite -- and ask question to whoever is equipped to answer it. This won't be Mr. Treanor. It's a practical matter. I was curious in my own mind as to what would happen when Mr. Treanor gave that answer on the transcript, that the -- that I thought that what would happen was that the -- when Mr. Treanor used the B/C/S word, that it would appear as a B/C/S word. If it appeared as an English word, it would rather destroy the point of the answers. And I see that what has happened at the moment, and this may be just be a temporary matter, that we get "[B/C/S spoken]." If that is at some point then substituted by the actual words being put in, there's absolutely no problem. I simply don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. From what I understand, it doesn't only say "[B/C/S spoken]," but also a sign appears after that which indicate that is there's still something to be filled in, as far as I understand. And this is confirmed by the registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, that's fine. It's simply a practical question, because I didn't know the way it worked, Your Honour. Clearly without that, the transcript wouldn't make a lot of sense to any later reader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. We'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And whenever you receive the transcript, you always can draw our attention to it if it doesn't appear --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in any way useful for the Defence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. But that does entirely clear up that point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It doesn't mean, I don't for a moment have to digest Mr. Treanor's answer, Your Honour, because I do. I may not be totally alone in that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is one other minor difference, if I may be allowed to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Please. Yes, of course. Thank you, Mr. Treanor. That's what I was inviting.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly version is written or rendered in the Ijekavian variant of the language, as opposed to the Gazette version, which is in Ekavian variant.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So in the -- does it -- what I'm getting at really is because of course we're aware of the underlying politics here. Is there, in your view, is there a discrepancy between what Dr. Karadzic was saying, and particularly the bit of that sentence "separation from the other two national communities, separation of states," as it appears in the B/C/S, and the B/C/S version of the Official Gazette. Is there in your view a discrepancy which is of political -- possible political significance?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the key word or words that are used here are "different." They have different meanings. They both undoubtedly have more than one meaning, more than one sense. And I would be fairly confident that some of those senses would overlap but some of them would not. Now, whether a native speaker - and here I would have to confess my linguistic limitations - especially a legal scholar would find an important difference in meaning between those two words in these contexts, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that's very fair, then, Mr. Treanor. So far as Dr. -- what Dr. Karadzic said is concerned - because after all, we can accept that's what the deputies heard on that particular day, after all, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So far as what Dr. Karadzic is saying is concerned, I think you said that that -- that the word there implied -- I don't know if the word used was "splitting," but splitting into two -- in fact, it would be three in this case. But that's not a relevant detail in a sense, linguistically, is it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, I don't know, whether that particular word can be used for splitting something into more than two parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It would have to be -- to put it that way, it would have to be, wouldn't it? Because otherwise it would make no sense at all in this context, because he's absolutely plainly and explicitly talking about three national communities. So it seems unlikely that Dr. Karadzic would have made such an elementary linguistic blunder as to use a word that could only apply to the splitting into two, when in fact there were three entities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you whether there's -- I have some difficulties in understanding what you say, but perhaps you could clarify this. If there are three parties and one party want to split up or -- from the other two, you could call them a bipartition, isn't it; the two on the one side and one on the other side? But since you -- you are confronting us and the witness with the linguistic blunder, as you say, I just wonder whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think on reflection, no. On reflection, hearing what Your Honour has said, no. I can see that it wouldn't necessarily be that. I see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It may be a splitting into two parties even though there are three nations involved. So I withdraw the suggestion, then, of it being a linguistic blunder.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's go back to it --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: As I understand it, Mr. Treanor, you're very fairly -- because after all, you -- although you speak a lot better B/C/S than most people round here who don't come from that part of the world, you acknowledge you're not a native speaker, so you're having difficulty, and as you frankly acknowledge, the limitations of your knowledge of the language don't really enable you to pronounce expertly on these nuances.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Is the -- what I really want to get to is how this ties in - and I don't want this to be a mystery - how this ties in with the Cutilheiro Plan, or I think when I used the phrase "Cutilheiro Plan" you said it was a framework for "negotiation." But again, as a shorthand label, I'm pretty sure it has been referred to as the "Cutilheiro Plan" in the past, and there's no secret what I mean. I would like to put the text of that plan -- it will have to be in English. Whether it was originally in English or French or both, I'm afraid at the moment I don't exactly know. Do you know, Mr. Treanor, whether the outcome of the meeting in Lisbon under the aegis of Mr. Cutilheiro was officially published in English or in French or in Portuguese, for that matter, or what?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there are two so-called agreements which I think you are referring to here. One is known as the Lisbon Agreement; the second one is known as the Sarajevo Agreement, both named after the site of the negotiations at which those agreements were reached. The Lisbon Agreement was reached in Lisbon in February 1992. And as you indicated yesterday, Mr. Izetbegovic later expressed reservations about that agreement and negotiations had to resume again, resulting in the Sarajevo Agreement of, I believe, the 18th of March, 1992, which suffered a similar fate. So we have two agreements, the Lisbon Agreement and the Sarajevo Agreement, and the Sarajevo Agreement was the -- chronologically, the latter of the two. So that would have been the point at which the negotiations broke down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you happen to know whether it was reached in one particular language only? And if so, which language?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes, the question. The version that I have seen is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. The version of -- well, perhaps both, but the Sarajevo Agreement, the version you've seen is in English.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the only version of that agreement that I may have seen is -- would have been published in the newspaper in B/C/S. But as far as the other one is concerned, I have seen an original document in English, and I believe both agreements were published in English in a large compendium of documents relating to the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. It's -- well, it's ultimately, if it becomes an issue, no doubt it is checkable. I apologise for not having been able to check it specifically in advance. And you referred to having read the Sarajevo Agreement in the newspaper in -- well, I don't suppose the newspaper regards it as B/C/S, but what we call B/C/S. But, of course, that itself could have been a translation.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I presume it was. I say if I saw it, and I can't quite recollect that specifically. But I do have in my mind's eye the Sarajevo Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Does it -- well, it follows -- is it the case that the -- this Cutilheiro or these Cutilheiro agreements, the Lisbon Agreement and the Sarajevo Agreement, are not in fact anywhere in the papers that you have produced for the purposes of your evidence to the Court?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I quoted from one or other or both of them. I had them in front of me at that time. I don't believe they were offered as exhibits, however. They certainly were not cited in our report.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. The -- it's -- really the purpose of my question is a practical one, which is that we were engaged in the not unfamiliar exercise to us of searching for something, not knowing for certain whether it was there at all, which mean that is the search can go on to infinity, since you don't know whether it's there. We weren't able to find it, so it look as if the reason we couldn't find it was actually because it wasn't there. Nice and simple.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I don't -- in a sense, there was an implicit invitation to anybody else in court who would say, "Well, I know exactly where it is and it's in Volume such and such," but nobody has leapt to their feet and said that, so I rather assume I can proceed on the footing that we didn't find it because it wasn't there. Which means, simply as a practical matter, then, it means, Your Honour, what I'm going to do is -- we have -- as you often do these days, we have been able to pull down from the Internet what appears to be the text of the Sarajevo Agreement. So, Your Honour, we've prepared copies of that -- yes. In fact, I should make it clear that what we have done is we have pulled down an English text of what appears on the face of it to be the Sarajevo Agreement. We've also been able to pull down a B/C/S version, but they're not the same. One is not -- there's no indication at all - and we suppose that neither is a translation of the other, because they come from independent sources on the Internet - so we naturally hope that they have some close relationship to each other, since they purport to be the same document. But they're not a translation, as far as we know, either of the other. Your Honour, my apologies that we haven't supplied this particular document in advance for the interpreters. We should have enough copies so that it's available to them now. The reason for that, I'm afraid, is simply the absence of any suitable gap between downloading the stuff from the Internet and the present moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, in respect of what you told us about the source of the documents you just provided, we'd rather give them two different numbers, because usually we'd use ".1" for the translation of another document, but since this is not, I'll ask Madam Registrar to provide numbers to these documents but unrelated numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The English version will be Defence Exhibit number D5, and the B/C/S version, Defence Exhibit number D6.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In the light of your answers a few minutes -- I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just ask if it's possible to have a couple of additional details about the provenance of these documents, in particular the websites from which they were procured. And although I realise things are moving quickly at this stage of the case, if it would be possible to be provided with these documents prior to the beginning of the courtroom session, it would be greatly appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As far as websites is concerned, let's not spend time on it at this moment, but I take it that you could provide Mr. Tieger during the break with the websites. And then if there's any problem remaining, then we'll hear about it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I have in mind to identify the website would be the right thing. Whether we can actually do it on the first break, I'm not actually sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We'll do it very soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we also have been provided with the map. Is the map attached to one of these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Philpott actually asked me. And the map is a separate -- came down as a separate item, again, from a different website, I suppose. It's from another source altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But is it related to -- are you going to tender it --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At the moment, perhaps I -- perhaps we can ignore it. I don't think it's not terribly exciting as it stands. I don't think it will cause any consternation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It doesn't get a number at this point. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We'll just leave that for the moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. In the light of your answers, your helpful answers about the terminology and Lisbon and Sarajevo, I suppose superficially confusing me, this particular printout is -- is headed "The Lisbon Agreement statement of principles," but then at the end it says "Sarajevo, 18th March 1992, as agreed." I suppose, I can just suggest, I suppose what happened, Mr. Treanor, is that having started off in Lisbon, it didn't get re-titled at the top, but it's got the Sarajevo date at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is this -- well, first of all, have you any reason -- perhaps you might need to take a minute or so just to take a look at it. Have new reason to doubt that this printout is a printout of the agreement reached in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you're referring to the English, I would have to say that I certainly could not accept it as the text that I am familiar with, given the rather glaring discrepancy you've already pointed out. In general terms, I think it is. But given that there is one glaring error in there, without further checking it I couldn't say that there aren't others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just ask: If these documents are presented as possibly the same, possibly translations, may I ask your attention, Mr. Stewart, to paragraph F, which takes two lines in the B/C/S version and some six lines in the English version. Then I further read --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say straightaway, I -- despite the injunction from Your Honour not to interrupt, may I? Because it may shorten things. Your Honour, I've just been informed -- I think I can answer Your Honour's question straight away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With respect. May I?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Because I also saw 28th of February, 1992, and the 18th of March, 1992 in the two different languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that Your Honour was going to point out some significant discrepancies. The information I've just been given is the English version is the Sarajevo Agreement; the B/C/S version is the Lisbon Agreement, so it's -- I was absolutely unaware of that until a moment ago. So that obviously explains why there may be significant discrepancies. My apologies for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. We are talk about two different documents in two different languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the probably the best thing for us to do is to -- when we, the first time we get the opportunity, is to see if we can download if English version of Lisbon and the B/C/S version of Sarajevo and then we'll have both pairs of agreements. My apologies for that. I simply had -- well, none of us did - up to that point I had no idea that what was apparently the same agreement was in fact the Lisbon version of B/C/S. For the -- that opportunity to get the B/C/S version of Sarajevo should arise pretty soon, Your Honour, but let's go ahead, if we may, on the basis of the English version. And there would be -- I take it there would be every opportunity for Mr. Treanor to check at some point whether anything special arose out of the B/C/S version of the Sarajevo Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Where we're getting to with all that complicated preamble about which agreement is what and what language it's in and so on, Mr. Treanor, is this: That -- the broad thrust of what I'm putting to you in relation to all these goals is that there is a close correlation between the six strategic goals as adopted and approved at the Bosnian Serb Assembly and the Cutilheiro Plan. That isn't a question at this point. That's just a basis so that you can understand where it is I'm going, then, with a series of questions. When we look at goal 1, which is expressed in the Official Gazette -- take one or the other -- as "Establish state borders separating the Serbian people from the other two communities." And in Dr. Karadzic's -- the translation of Dr. Karadzic's version, the first such goal is "Separation from the other two national communities." So there's not a lot of difference in English, despite what you've said about B/C/S. That broadly reflects, doesn't it, what we see in A1 of the Cutilheiro document in front of us - and I'm talking about the English version now, the Sarajevo Agreement.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to make sure that I've understood properly, I understand the question to be whether the first strategic goal as set forth in the Assembly session version and the Gazette version corresponds to point A1 in the Sarajevo Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer to that would have to be no, there is a tremendous difference. The strategic goals call clearly for the creation of a state boundary between the Serbian entity and -- on the one hand, and the other two entities, on the other. The premise of the Sarajevo Agreement is that Bosnia and Herzegovina would itself be a state composed of three constituent units. So that is a very important difference between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is there -- and, of course, you do have the, Mr. Treanor, whatever the precise wording of the B/C/S version of the Cutilheiro document, there would be no issue between us. It's quite clear that the Sarajevo Agreement did proceed on the basis that Bosnia and Herzegovina would be a single state, so we don't have to debate that. Is it crystal clear to you that what Dr. Karadzic is talking about in the Assembly on the 12th of May, 1992 involves separate states? From an international point of view, that would be.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly take that to be his meaning there and the meaning of the Gazette item. Those two documents, of course, do not stand alone. We have the Declaration of Independence, in fact, of the Serbian Republic in early April, from all of which it appears that it was their intention -- and an intention in their view already carried out -- that they be a separate state from the rest of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So far as the second strategic goal is concerned, now, that is the establishment - and it's summarised in the Official Gazette as "Setting up a corridor between Semberija and Krajina." And that is summarised in those simple terms by Dr. Karadzic at the beginning of what he said about this, at page 127 -- I'm sorry, tab 127 in bundle 12, page 13 of the English but probably by now on page 8 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The second -- and Dr. Karadzic said -- and after all, it's quite a long time since we looked at this originally in your evidence, Mr. Treanor. The second strategic goal: "It seems to me as a corridor between Semberija and Krajina, that is something for which we may be forced to sacrifice something here and there, but this is of the utmost strategic importance for the Serbian people because it integrates the Serbian lands not only of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina but Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina with Serbia, and the Serbian Krajina with Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia. So that is a very important strategic goal which we have to achieve because there will be no Krajina, Bosnian Krajina, Serbian Krajina or alliance of Serbian states if we do not secure that corridor which will integrate us and give us unimpeded flow from one part of our state with another." If we look at the Cutilheiro Plan, as I've labeled it, A1, that we looked at a moment ago: "Bosnia and Herzegovina would be a state composed of --" and leave aside your comment on the first goal -- "composed of three constituent units based on national principles and taking into account economic, geographic, and other criteria." And may be also look at E, a definition of the constituent units: "A working group will be established in order to define the territory of the constituent units based on national principles, taking into account economic, geographical, and other criteria." So a repetition of those criteria as have been stated in A1, "A map based on the national relative will be the basis of work in the working group and will be subject only to amendments justified by the above-mentioned criteria." Now, the -- Mr. Treanor, would you say -- of course it may not have been easy, but that the goal expressed as the second strategic goal was, in principle and subject to negotiation, consistent with the principles stated in the Cutilheiro Plan in A1 and E?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would say that the achievement of the second goal is extremely problematic on the basis of the Sarajevo Agreement. If I'm not mistaken, and this would be reflected in the records of the sessions of the Bosnian Serb Assembly especially in February and March 1992, it was the Bosnian Serb delegation that had insisted on the primacy of ethnic criteria in the delimitation of the entities. So whether they would be in a strong position to push for some other criteria in particular areas is open to question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: But if we look at the map of the Lisbon Agreement that you have presented me, we can see on that map --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This is the map that I said a few minutes ago I put on one side. You've got it, so we had better introduce it formally, since you now wish to refer to it, Mr. Treanor. It came from me; I accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I think it would get numbered D7, Madam Registrar, if I'm correct. And that is a map with words written in B/C/S. And you tell us, Mr. Stewart, that it is an attachment to the Sarajevo or to the Lisbon Agreement? As far as I can see, on the bottom it only says that it's a Cutilheiro map, but that doesn't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's the -- I'm instructed that it's the - from Mr. Krajisnik, Your Honour - that it's the Sarajevo Agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor said Lisbon, but I think at least just because he assumed it was Lisbon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm under the impression that this map came from the same source that the B/C/S version of the Lisbon Agreement came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It didn't in fact, Mr. Treanor. It's understandable that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's be -- if we do not know whether this map belongs to the Lisbon or the Sarajevo Agreement, then I wouldn't mind that reference is made to this map, but then, rather, let's say map D7, whatever it represents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. We'll double-check, Your Honour, what it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So map D7, Mr. Treanor, you were going to make some comment based on map D7.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm simply using this map because it's the one before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I think it illustrates the point I want to make. There are of course other maps I think some of which may have been used in the course of my testimony, but this map clearly does not provide for a corridor of the type described in strategic goal number 2. I would call the Court's attention to the top of the map, the black area, which is Croatian in the middle of the northern boundary. Under that there's the white area, in which is the Muslim part. And on either side, the striped portions which are Serbian. So this particular map, I guess we don't know what its status was, but if this is the basis of negotiations, it does not provide for a corridor. I believe that this map reflects the ethnic majorities in the various municipalities. If not, we can always turn to such a map. But that demographic situation in that particular part of Bosnia makes the realisation -- again, makes the realisation of a Serbian corridor on the basis of ethnic composition extremely problematic. The other two national communities seem to dominate in that area, and presumably, it would have been very loathe to cede territory to the Serbian entity in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is there in fact, just to clarify -- I think so in fact you did describe it really very clearly, Mr. Treanor, but so there's no scope of misunderstanding, this is what I would call the sort of large blob of black towards the top right-hand or north-east part of the map. That's Croatian, or that's Croat territory.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then as the legends -- even I can handle that Cyrillic -- as the legends tell us, the horizontal stripe of -- that's Serbian territory, and the white is Muslim. And then we've got Sarajevo, of course, as the diagonal hatched part. Is there -- it appears that there is a small gap between the top -- the north-eastern Serb territory, which is -- that is -- probably that's Semberija.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Semberija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, Semberija. And then of course the very large south -- north-western Serb territory, that's Krajina.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We've got a whole lot of Croat territory. And then there looks to be a tiny little gap. So in fact -- is it correct that between Semberija and that north-eastern Croat territory there is in fact a small, relatively small bit of Muslim-occupied territory?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There is territory there which is indicated as Muslim here. I wouldn't say particularly small.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it's small, especially when combined with the fact that the Croatian territory seems to enter into it. So there's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think I introduced the word "relatively" because I'd realised that it's -- you can't just jump over it on the ground, Mr. Treanor. So clearly on any footing some cooperation, whether it's by negotiation, exchange, or whatever, some cooperation is needed in practice with both Muslims and Croats in order to establish such a corridor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, what I wasn't suggesting to you, in fact, Mr. Treanor, was that the Lisbon or the Sarajevo Agreements, any of the Cutilheiro proposals, plans, frameworks actually specifically provided for such a corridor. What I was putting to you was something different, which was as a goal for the Serbs it is at least in principle consistent with the notion of territories being defined to take into account economic, geographical, and other criteria.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly would have been open to them on the basis of this agreement as -- this agreement being the basis of negotiations, to enter into negotiations for accord on that basis, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So far as the third goal or the third objective is concerned, again this involves a corridor, and it's described in the Official Gazette as "Establish a corridor in the Drina River Valley; that is, eliminate the Drina as a border separating Serbian states." And the, roughly speaking -- and I think roughly is perhaps enough for our purposes, but you can say if it isn't. If we look at the same map, D7, the Serb territory in the north-east, Semberija, that we were talking about, does the Drina River at the border you're talking about, it runs along the eastern side of that top north-eastern swath of Serb territory; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm sorry, I'm preoccupied with another issue because I've noticed there's a discrepancy in the wording between the two versions of this goal, which is a matter you were interested in before in connection with goal number 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I remain interested, Mr. Treanor. Should we just park that point for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This section of the map does provide for a very narrow, at two points, corridor, and that is the first part of the goal between the northern section, Semberija, and going all the way down to the southern section which is Eastern Herzegovina. There is continuous territory there, apparently. I'm looking at the northern bottleneck, which is a little obscured, and there's a similar bottleneck in the south. Now, the Drina does not form the border -- the eastern border of Bosnia along the entire length of the eastern border of Bosnia, and I must confess my geographical knowledge or memory is a bit deficient, but I can see that part of the Muslim area here does directly abut on the eastern border of Bosnia. Whether at that point the Drina is in fact the border, I don't know. We'd have to look at a topographical map to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think what I was putting to you, Mr. -- you're absolutely right, Mr. Treanor, it doesn't -- and I wasn't suggesting that the Drina River goes all along the eastern border there of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It just -- it's just not that long a river. What I am saying is that if we go above what you described as the two bottlenecks, the northern bottleneck of that swath of Serb territory that goes from north all the way to the south, the northern bottleneck, if we go above that, and then it -- the Serb territory broadens out, that the Drina River goes along much of the eastern border of that bit of Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the issue here is whether it goes along the eastern border of the Muslim bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then -- yes, and then down -- not right down into all that southern Serb territory but along that eastern border, and then -- well, I don't know how far down it goes, Mr. Treanor. In fact, it -- yes, it looks -- it does in fact go all the way round that little inlet, we see, to the south of the Muslim territory, where it joins along the eastern border more Serb territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you: Do we have to continue with this conversation between two gentlemen where the Drina River is? I mean, if you want to draw the attention to the Drina River, the Chamber would like to be presented with a map or whatever, or one of the maps that is already in evidence. But I've listened now for almost one and a half, two minutes to where the Drina River might have been. Mr. Treanor, could you indicate where in accordance with the third objective, where the corridor was supposed to be established on this map? Can you indicate that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The map could be put on the ELMO so that you could point at it. Oh, it's already on the ELMO. I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have to admit that would require a bit of interpretation on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you indicate that on a map which is more detailed in geographical terms. If we would have another map, could you say it's to be located there or there; that's how we have to understand the third objective.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, as I say, I would have to interpret a bit. But my interpretation of this goal is that the border would run the entire length of this eastern border.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be the corridor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of the Serbian entity --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And where -- yes. Well, it's clear to me now what is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Allowing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you indicate where exactly that corridor -- because we're talking about "Establish a corridor in the Drina River Valley" -- where would that corridor be needed and to be established? Could you indicate this on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I made allusion to that earlier, Your Honour. To my mind, this goal seems to have two parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Establishing a border for the Serbian entity along the entire length of the Drina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And indeed along the entire length of the existing BH border, which would give it a border with Serbia and Montenegro, along the entire length of that border, perhaps leaving Muslim enclaves, as Dr. Karadzic refers to, in this area but enclaves that would not be on that border. Now, that's the border -- that's the border part. The corridor part refers to having, I believe, a continuous connection between this part of the country and this part of the country, Eastern Herzegovina being a very important region for the Serbs. So they wanted a continuous connection territorially down the middle, so to speak, that's between bits of Muslim territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if I may interrupt you, on this map the corridor from objective 2 seems not to be there, in terms of this map, whereas the connection to be established by the corridor of the third objective seems to be present on this map. Is that a correct understanding, although there are some bottlenecks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, barely. Yes, with two bottlenecks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we look at the Cutilheiro Plan, the Sarajevo Agreement, the English version, we've got A1, which we've already looked at: "Take account of economic, geographic, and other criterias in establishing the three constituent units." We've got D2, towards the end of D2, because that's quite a long provision, the last few lines on the third page of the printout: "A constituent unit may establish and may maintain relations and links with the other republics and with organisations in them provided that these relations and links are consistent with the independence and integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina." And then -- no, stop there, A1 and D2. And this -- I suggest to you that the elimination of the Drina as a border between Serbian states, which in this case would be the Republika Srpska as it came to be known and Serbia, is consistent with the underlying principles in those parts of the Cutilheiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, that's not what's being referred to here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you regard this as more limited, do you, in some way?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when it says "establish and maintain relations and links" I take that to mean something on the order of diplomatic, political, economic, military, whatever, relations and links; the links perhaps referring to communications links, roads -- roads, air service, that sort of thing. But I don't think the focus here is on territorial issues per se.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, wouldn't -- well, wouldn't the elimination of the Drina as a border separating Serbian states be entirely consistent with the notion of, admittedly, close relations and links?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. That's why they wanted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. But that's what I'm saying. That's what the Cutilheiro document is saying. It talks about establishing and maintaining relations and links with the other republics and with organisations in them. Those links can include the elimination of a border, can't they?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the elimination of -- well, I don't think you mean elimination of a border. The establishment of a border between two states can facilitate the establishment and maintenance of relations and links, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, let me give you a simple illustration. Although they remain independent sovereign states, in many respects borders between the member states of the European Union have been eliminated, haven't they? There's no passport control, for example.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: What the Bosnian Serb leaders wanted to do basically was eliminate a state border between themselves and Serbia or not -- I guess in their terms they did not want to see the establishment of a state border between themselves and Serbia. They were in Yugoslavia. Serbia was in Yugoslavia. And the only border between them was what they referred to as an administrative border. They did not want to see a state border established between them, which is in my understanding of the basis of these negotiations precisely what would have been established, which was something they had brought themselves to accept that they would have to live with a state border between themselves and Serbia and Montenegro for at least a certain period of time. But, on the other hand, they wanted the ability to establish various sorts of relations and links with Serbia and Montenegro and organisations within them. And I dare say that the leaders of the HDZ wanted to do the same thing in regards to Croatia. That is what is being referred to here. The establishment of -- and the corridor along the Drina -- and here we get into the difference in wording between the two versions of this goal. But if we just take that goal to mean what I have indicated, that they would have a border along the length of the eastern border, giving them contiguous territory with Serbia and Montenegro, that would certainly facilitate the establishment of such relations and links, which is why they very much wanted to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, it may be -- well, we know what ideally from their point of view the Bosnian Serbs wanted. That's clear. It's equally clear, I'd suggest, that Dr. Karadzic and others realised perfectly well at this point, didn't they, that getting exactly what you wanted was unlikely?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this particular point in time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But the --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular feature of the plan, if the Court will recall the discussions in the Bosnian Serb Assembly from late February 1992, was sold, if I can use that expression as you have, to the Assembly on the basis that what was being agreed to as a whole within the framework of the negotiations at that time was only a first step toward their ultimate goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the -- perhaps the point is what in the third strategic goal is actually inconsistent with the principles in the Cutilheiro, the Sarajevo Agreement?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, here we get into the issue that I've alluded to a couple of times, the difference in the wording between the two versions of that goal, which also could bring us to a question of the interpretation of one of those wordings. In the Assembly version, there is reference to "the elimination of the Drina as a border between two worlds." In the Gazette version, there is reference to "the elimination of the Drina as a border between Serbian states." That certainly says to me that they wanted to be in the same state with Serbia and Montenegro; that was their goal. That goal, as I think I have indicated more than once, would have been at sharp variance with the basis of the Cutilheiro negotiations which foresaw the maintenance of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state. I'm looking for some of the wording. Well, at the beginning of day one: "Bosnia and Herzegovina would be a state composed of three entities." So goal 3 seems to fly directly in the face of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no -- I'm sorry, there's no magically convenient point to break in this questioning, so I'm entirely in Your Honour's hands as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll -- if this is a suitable moment, we'll adjourn until five minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, have you -- have you ever read a book written by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic? It's got a very simple title, I think, in English. "Memoirs" I think is all it's called.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What I'm going to do at the moment is we -- I haven't copied the whole book. I'm sure we could get hold of a copy of the book. What we have done is we've copied a single page. It's written, not surprisingly, in B/C/S. No, I haven't done a translation, Your Honour, because what I'm going to put to Mr. -- well, I haven't done a translation because I couldn't do a translation, but apart from that. We haven't got a translation because what I'm going to do at this stage is put to the witness a short passage from the book itself, and depending where we go with this translation in his answer, it may be absolutely unnecessary to obtain any separate translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The passage that is relevant is the -- just the very last paragraph, and in fact there's a particular bit within that. So, Mr. Treanor, may I invite you to give us your translation of the last paragraph on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I should say, Your Honour, I apologise for the underlining and marking and so on, but in the end we came to the conclusion that it didn't really signify anything very much or wasn't tendentious in any particular way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Shouldn't we ask the witness to read it in B/C/S slowly so that the interpreters can provide us with a translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. That's a very helpful suggestion, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, please read it in the original language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And for these circumstances, usually it's better to have already a copy. If there is any spare copy for the booth, then it's easier for them to translate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We did it, Your Honour, this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In such a situation, a sovereign B and H in a free community for us is the only guarantee for life in dignity and freedom and not only for the Muslim people but also for the Serb and Croat people. In view of the composition of the population, such Bosnia and Herzegovina must have special relations with Serbia on the one hand and Croatia on the other, and regardless of whether these two republics, states would be mutually linked and in what way. We believe that this can be resolved. "Serbs must not have the feeling that they are separated from Serbia by a state border or Croats separated from Croatia. Therefore, there should be no passports for Serbs on the Drina or for the Croats on the Una."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And that, Mr. Treanor, I can tell you was said by Mr. Izetbegovic at the First Congress of the SDA in 1991. Looking again at D2 of the Cutilheiro document and particularly the last sentence, and looking at what Mr. Izetbegovic has said there against strategic goal number 3, would you agree that what is being talked about in strategic goal number 3, "elimination of the Drina as a border separating Serbian states," now appears to be consistent both with D2 in the Cutilheiro document, the Sarajevo Agreement, and with what Mr. Izetbegovic himself had expressly said in December 1991?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. I think at this point I'm being asked to compare three and possibly four documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think three at the moment, but four if -- yes, four if we take --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- both the minutes of the Serb Assembly and the Official Gazette version. Yes, it would be four, Mr. Treanor. But let me perhaps -- I hope I rephrase it sufficiently closely to the way I phrased it the first time. It's that in the -- that the strategic goals, whether they're expressed -- the strategic goal 3, whether it's expressed in the form as at the meeting of the Serb Assembly, Dr. Karadzic's version on the day or in the form subsequently published in the Official Gazette, that strategic goal is consistent both with the Sarajevo Agreement and with what Mr. Izetbegovic himself had expressly said.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just to remind myself, if not to remind the Court, strategic goal 3, the Gazette version refers to "The establishment of a corridor in the valley of the River Drina, that is, the elimination of the Drina as a border between Serbian states," which I have -- take to mean that the Bosnian Serb Republic would become part of the same state as Serbia and Montenegro. If we turn to point A2 in the Sarajevo Agreement, we can read that, according to this provision, "Bosnia and Herzegovina would continue to have its existing borders and neither the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina nor the governments of the constituent units will encourage or support claims to any part of its territories by neighbouring states." In D2, we read that "a constituent unit may establish and maintain relations and links with the other republics and with organisations in them provided that these relations and links are consistent with the independence and integrity of Bosnia and Herzegovina." In the Izetbegovic document, we see reference at the beginning to "a sovereign BH." We then see reference further on to "such a BH having special relations with Serbia on the one hand and Croatia on the other," irrespective of whether these two republics are linked with each other or not or indeed are independent states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, may I ask one thing I'm wondering. Mr. Tieger, because I see that at this moment the Defence is seeking to establish that the six strategic goals are not inconsistent with the Cutilheiro Plan, whatever, or the documents, or the book of Mr. Izetbegovic. Let me first ask: Is it the position of the Prosecution that the six strategic goals are inconsistent or irreconcilable with the Cutilheiro Plan or with the book of Mr. Izetbegovic -- the position of Mr. Izetbegovic at that time, or -- what's the position of the Prosecution? Because I can imagine -- let me try to make a comparison. If I would say I'd love to earn a million dollars and -- or at least to have a million dollars and then later on I either work hard and I earn those million dollars or I find another way by stealing them, what is our situation? Is it a position of the Prosecution that there's anything wrong with the starting point, or is it the position of the Prosecution that this starting point might explain what later happened, that is, either work hard or go out at night and steal a million dollars? What's the position of the Prosecution? Because I wonder whether there's any disagreement on this issue and then, of course, the strategic goals as, well, some relevant point in the history. Mr. Tieger, could you answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm afraid I won't be able to answer that as comprehensively as I'd like. I certainly understand the point the Court is driving at, and I think that's a useful insight. What I can say are two things, I think: Number one, with respect to that particular perspective, starting from a particular objective, a particular motivation and the distinction between that motivation and the manner in which it may be achieved, I think we probably could come to some kind of consensus with the Defence. At the same time, I think the way the issue has been framed by the Defence in the course of the examination this afternoon reflects the fact that there are distinctions to be made, as emphasised by Mr. Treanor in his examination. That's all a way of saying that yes, I think if we sat down, a good deal of the consensus that the Court appears to see could be reached, but that discussion hasn't taken place. We were just presented with the issue of the Cutilheiro Plan, as you saw, this afternoon. And again, as it was framed in the course of the examination, I think significant distinctions were addressed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, therefore, there are two issues: The first one is that at least to say the language, in the six strategic goals, even if in their different version is not exactly the same and if you compare them with other documents, there are differences in language and it's a matter of interpretation on what exactly these differences in language stand for and whether this is an indication whether or not it's inconsistent, it's entirely clear to the Chamber at this moment that -- the point the Defence wants to make, and we are just -- I think at this moment at the third objective. There are six further to go. Perhaps if you would have in mind that it's clear to the Chamber what point you'd like to make. Perhaps it could be made a bit quicker. Of course, you're dependent on the answers of the witness. But if you look at the lines the questions take in the transcript and the lines the answer take in the transcript, then I couldn't say that the witness is to be blamed for the length of time. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, it would be -- if I could write the answers as well, Your Honour, that would -- that would really speed things along.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would. Yes. Yes, I do understand. But unfortunately you cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It would be nice to earn a million dollars as well. But it's been done before. Your Honour, yes, in so far -- I will proceed a little bit on the third objective because it --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In considering the third objective, Mr. Treanor, you -- and in responses you're really proceeding from the footing, well, the Serbs here are looking for separate state independence of the Serb Republic within BH, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the implication of the wording of the third goal and this Gazette version seems to me to be precisely that and not only the wording of that goal but, of course, their action in declaring independence in early April, that they wanted a separate state.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just let me ask you this, then: If they had a separate state, why would they need to be talking about the Drina River as a specific strategic objective at all? Because if they're next door to Serbia and they are an independent state, then if Serbia will have them, they can have Serbia and that's the end of the matter. They've got a deal.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Karadzic laid that out in his explanation in regard to the third strategic goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. But what I'm putting to you there, Mr. Treanor, is that entirely separately from the question of whether the Serb Republic is a separate state, the third goal makes sense when set alongside the Cutilheiro document and Mr. Izetbegovic's statement. It makes sense even in the context of the Serb Republic remaining part of what single overall state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never did finish comparing the documents. I don't think that goal 3, as I think I indicated before the break, is -- it would be difficult to achieve within the framework of the Cutilheiro -- of the Sarajevo Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as far as the Izetbegovic document is concerned, which I was asked about before, we can see that there is no reference to any constituent -- separate constituent units within BH. There's only a reference to a separate BH -- a sovereign BH, I'm sorry, a sovereign BH -- having relations, special relations with Croatia and Serbia. And there's -- the only particular that's mentioned there is eliminating the feeling that Serbs and Croats might have that the state border which would exist would separate them from Serbia or Croatia, and the willingness to overcome this feeling by letting them cross the border without passports. This is quite a different thing than eliminating the border between two states and between two entities, the Bosnian Serb Republic and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as it existed on the 12th of May, 1992, and thereby becoming one state. Let us recall that the Constitution of the Bosnian Serb Republic defines that republic as part of Yugoslavia. This is far different from what Mr. Izetbegovic is talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think we may have got to the point where we would move into the realm of argument and interpretation of documents, and so I won't proceed with further questions in relation to the third goal. So far as the fourth goal is concerned, establishing a border on the Una and Neretva River, is it correct, Mr. Treanor, that in the Cutilheiro document, as agreed in Sarajevo, the Una River was in fact marked as the border of a Serb or the Serb constituent unit within Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the only map I have before me is the one you submitted to me, and I really can't tell definitely from this map whether the separation line in the extreme north-west is along the Una. I rather suspect that it isn't, because I think this map is probably based on the municipal boundaries, and the Una did cut through certain municipalities, notably Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The position is you're not actually -- you're not in a position this afternoon to tell us yourself whether it was or it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of this map, yeah. Yes. I can't say whether this map -- I cannot definitely say whether this map indicates a border along the Una.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you can't recall yourself from your previous reading of documents --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my recollection --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- whether it did or it didn't.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- of these maps is that they were based on -- and they were based on the municipal boundaries. And let's remember that the maps were only supposed to be, as the agreement, a framework for negotiation. So it would have been open to the Bosnian Serbs in the course of the negotiations to -- if -- well, to seek a border on the Una, which would not have involved a very large shifting of whatever border is in fact indicated on that particular map, because we're not talking about great distances up there, either between the external boundaries of the municipalities I'm referring to in the Una or indeed, the length of the Una River itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I can wrap the remainder of these points on the strategic goals into one simple question. Is it the position that however difficult or easy it might have been, no part of goals 4, 5, or 6 was inconsistent with the Sarajevo Agreement? And you may need a moment just to refresh your memory as to goals 4, 5, and 6.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think I'm ready. 4, 5, and 6. We have discussed the Una already.
