The Neretva, again if we look at this map, the border of the Serbian entity on the map doesn't even come close to the Neretva River, especially in its lower reaches. We had a - thank you - we had a telephone conversation that I presented between certain Bosnian Serb leaders and certain Bosnian Croat leaders in which they discussed the issue of the Neretva, and the Court may recall that the Croats found it very amusing that the Bosnian Serbs would even pretend to claim territory up to the Neretva River. So I would say that this particular goal within the framework of the Sarajevo Agreement would have been a very difficult, if not an impossible realisation. Again, bearing in mind that this is a framework for negotiations and anyone presumably -- any party to those negotiations could bring up any issue they would like. That is goal 4. Goal 5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 6 is access of --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: 5 is Sarajevo and 6 is access to the sea.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo, goals 5. There doesn't seem to be any particular reference in the Sarajevo Agreement to Sarajevo; the map has indicated as a separate area. Goal 5 calls for its division. So that would seem to be a difference there. Under goal 5, in its Gazette version, Sarajevo would be divided indeed between two states, whereas under the Sarajevo Agreement framework it would of course be within one state. Goal 6 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, you say 5 involves -- just pausing a moment -- 5 involves, you say, division into two states?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, goal 5 in its Gazette version reads: "With a view to the city of Sarajevo --" I'm sorry -- "the division of the city of Sarajevo into a Serbian and Muslim part and the establishment in each of those parts of effective state authority."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know about the B/C/S, Mr. Treanor, but I suggest to you that read into the trade "state authorities" a division into two separate independent states is reading an awful lot, that "state authorities" simply mean in effect public authorities, government organs. It would mean that in each part you've got to have some effective authorities running the place.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, the Bosnian Serb Republic had declared its independence at the beginning of April. Its Constitution stated that it was a part of Yugoslavia. Goal 3 has called for the elimination of the Drina as a border between Serbian states. I would infer from that that the Serbian portion of Sarajevo was going to be within the Serbian state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to clarify the record, Your Honour - and it may be helpful - I think the witness spoke about division between two states, and I believe he was essentially quoted back by Mr. Stewart as saying "division into two states." Perhaps that's the source of some confusion here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I recognise the fine distinction. I had thought a few minutes ago, but perhaps I was overoptimistic -- I had thought a few minutes ago when I put my compendious question to you that there was nothing inconsistent with goals 4, 5, and 6 with the Sarajevo Agreement that I had got a yes. But it now seems that I haven't got a yes, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought I'd been giving my answer to that point by point. I'm at point 6, strategic goal 6 right now. If I could address that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? I thought I had got a yes, so I'm just clarifying. You will have to take them one by one, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. If Mr. Treanor would deal with objective 6, we could then see whether you would have a yes on the sixth objective. But on 4 and 5, as far as I understand you, Mr. Treanor, there's no yes that there -- to the question of Mr. -- that they are consistent with the Cutilheiro Plan.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I had lost the question, and now I understand from you that the question is are they consistent with the Cutilheiro Plan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think as a matter of fact, that you said Una River not considerably different; Neretva River, certainly; Sarajevo, it's the division into two states with all the subtleties that have been added; and now we're up to strategic objective 6, I think. But if, Mr. Stewart if you are, by not having a yes on all three you would refrain from the sixth, then we'll hear from you. Otherwise, I think we are at the sixth objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I'm happy to go on to the sixth. I've got the position -- yes. Even if I'd then get tempted to go back, let's go on to 6, as His Honour suggests, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The sixth objective is simply stated in the Gazette version as an outlet of the Republika Srpska, as it's called here, a name which was not adopted until August 1992, an outlet to the sea. Dr. Karadzic in his remarks refers to this goal, although it is the last goal, as very important. He makes clear in his remarks that what is being referred to by an outlet is not some sort of commercial agreement for the use of a free port or something of that nature but is, in fact, a territorial claim against Croatia. As he explains this goal, they want a territorial outlet to the sea through territory which up to that point and indeed continues to be part of the Republic of Croatia. This is something that has absolutely no place in the Sarajevo Agreement whatsoever. Croatia was not a party to the negotiations, and none of the parties to the negotiations could have conceded that to the Bosnian Serb party to those negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, the conclusion from that, though, is that there is no inconsistency between the sixth goal and the Sarajevo Agreement, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose if you take the absence of something from it, in that light, yes, you could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Putting it another way, if the Serbs can sort it out with Croatia, it's no particular concern for the Muslims in particular in BH, is it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they had come to an agreement that that did not impinge upon what the Muslims considered to be their interest, then yes, I believe that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can I just go back to number 4, though, because I'm trying to narrow it down, the differences between us. So far as number 4 is concerned, the two rivers, the -- leaving aside the question of whether these things are easy or difficult to achieve, I do press you that however difficult they might have been, there is no inconsistency between either limb of the fourth goal and the Sarajevo Agreement.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. If the other parties had agreed to that, again -- and as I said several times, the agreement was a basis for negotiations and they could have negotiated anything, and -- that is, the Bosnian Serbs could have raised any issue in the negotiations, except presumably an outlet to the sea -- and it would have been open to the other sides, to other parties to that negotiation to concede their demands.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could we just look at the document that's at tab 127 of Volume 12.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could we go to page 50 of the English version. I'm sorry, I don't know what page it is in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Perhaps if you wouldn't mind just going back to the previous page, because we see it's where Mr. Krajisnik starts speaking, towards the top of page 49. And he's moving that we adopt the conclusions. Dr. Karadzic has had quite a lot to say. Then Mr. Krajisnik -- do you see that? Momcilo Krajisnik: "I move that we adopt the conclusions"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's page 50?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's at 49. I moved back one page from page 50. 49 now.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the top or the bottom?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Towards the top. Momcilo Krajisnik: "I move that we adopt --"

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, the very top. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's page 37 in B/C/S. "I move that we adopt the conclusions. We've heard quite a few proposals. I should try to make a summary, but before that I want to say that we would need some time but we will get used to the generals and the generals will get used to us. In any case, the most important thing that we all mean well." Then he -- I think you highlighted a passage towards the bottom, about ten lines up: "As for the goals, I would just like to offer an explanation, since I've also taken part in adopting these goals. We must make a choice regarding one thing." Then he says: "The first goal is the most important one. And in relation to all other goals, all other goals are sub-items of the first one. Have we finally decided to separate from the remaining two national communities, we can part from them if Bosnia and Herzegovina is to be torn into three parts. What kind of share will each of us get all depends on the elements I presented. That's why it would be good, my dear gentlemen, to take care to leave enough space for division. I shall be a bit immodest; do not hold it against me. We once placed the option on our agenda of making a map and should anyone offer us 80 per cent of the territory, we still would not be able to work out a partition." And then -- I want to try to avoid simply reading the whole lot -- but he goes on about ten lines down saying that "wherever there were Serbs, it was Serbian territory that represented a mobilisation of the entire Serbian people. We shall in an organised and fair manner provide our people with a roof over their heads. Resettle them if need be; we shall not put them in a genocidal position. I know that I myself may remain in" -- well, Muslimania, he calls it. It has an unfortunate ring in English, but we see what he means. "But I have no regrets. But the rest of the people should be happy. Now we can see which territories are free. We are all fighting for self-contained territories of a piece with the corridors so that all of us will be in a single area that is linked with Serbian and Montenegro. utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe I do. I believe this copy of the document came from or was found in a collection that we referred to as the Sarajevo collection. The Sarajevo collection represents documents which were seized by the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina after the commencement of the war in -- at the commencement of the war in early April, so therefore sometime after that. I'm not sure exactly when, for which lot of documents. They seized many documents in different locations. One of those locations was the office of the SDS and I believe that this document was found among those documents. During the course of the war, the documents, as far as I know, were in the custody of the State Security Service - I'm trying to get the right name at that time - at that time, it was still known as the State Security Service of, at that point in time, the Republic of BH. During the time that the officials of the State Security Service had custody of the documents, they created an inventory of those documents, in the course of which work they developed a classification system, if I may put it that way, to identify each of the documents in the inventory. In the upper right-hand corner of the middle document, which we see on the screen, you can see the letter "B" -- "B-1" apparently 1, and something after -- I can't -- the one below looks like "K 2," something of that nature. And then we see the numeral "26," which I'm trying to get to. They classified the documents in the following fashion: They put various documents in various places in their office. These documents wound up in what is referred to as Cabinet B, hence the "B" in the upper right-hand corner. The documents within the cabinet were, of course, arrayed on the shelves. The Roman numeral I refers to the shelf number; that is the top shelf. The next letter refers to a folder that was on that shelf, and they were designated A, B, C, going through the alphabet. Occasionally there are two folders with the same letter, so you might say K1 or K2, if that's what this is. And, of course, they used the letters of the B/C/S alphabet, so you'll have designations such as NJ, which is one letter in B/C/S, or LJ, and of course the letters with the diacritics. Now, within each folder they designated each document according to the order the document was found in within that folder, working from the top. So this is document number 26 within the folder that has that designation B1, K2, whatever it is. Unfortunately from various points of view, they chose to write all this information on the document itself. So that's what the various handwritten markings at the top of the document indicate. Now, there came a point in time - I think I know what your next question might be - there came a point in time when they took certain of the documents out of their folders, having identified them as being particularly relevant or particularly important, and they put them in another folder, the important document folder, and they numbered them all over again within that folder. And so that's what I believe the number "24" refers to. Well, let me just finish the story by saying that the originals -- that is, those documents, the ones that they found and had in their offices and were working with and made an inventory of and designated in this fashion -- are, in principle, now, in this building in the Evidence Unit. Now, of course, since we're talking about documents that were seized at various offices and indeed residences and such, many of those documents were themselves photocopies. So we find within that collection as "original documents," that is, original as seized documents, which are in fact photocopies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Treanor. That -- it's an important thing to clear up. But you certainly have cleared it up.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing I can say is that this appears to be a photocopy of one generation or another of a document on which those handwritten notations may have been made at one time or another. utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]

utterances.text: No. I think it's an important distinction to draw, Your Honour. And you're correct, it's not an issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And I think the manuscript amendment. Because that was the one that had -- sorry, annotations. That was the one that had the manuscript annotations. But those appear to be the same as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I couldn't see that, because I've seen only one copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They certainly appear to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's take it as that being the position for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me just say two quick things, if I may: Number one, it may be significant -- it would be significant if they came from two different places if there were two different documents and the manuscript notations might indicate that; and secondly, I just wonder if Mr. Treanor is the appropriate person and this is the appropriate time to be make those particular distinctions, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I have no problem with that, Your Honour. I was actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be very practical. I do understand that all the document that is have been presented now with or without handwriting and copied, with the same handwriting on them or not, is the same typewritten documents, that the parties do not disagree on that. And what the relevance of this fact now established is, we'll learn that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then this is -- it's getting fainter now. This is a fainter copy of again, this number 96. Again, it looks essentially to be the same document or derived from the same source as the previous two.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Wherever it gets us to, Mr. Treanor, would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's the same typewritten document. The quality of the copying is very bad. It appears to bear the same handwritten notations, except on the front page where it does not have the numbers at the top that I referred to on the one copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. And then a further document. Perhaps we could have the -- you'll be relieved to know, no plastic folders at the moment with these -- Perhaps we could have the front page, the cover page on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The front page of this has got all sorts of stamps and numbers and so on which are slightly different, aren't they, from what we've seen before, --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- Mr. Treanor? Could you just give us a run-through what we see there.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I've ever seen this one before. It's number 104. It has a stamp right above the copy number, and it's the stamp of the Institute for the Investigation of Crimes Against Humanity of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Sarajevo. It has some sort of registration number within that stamp, and then below the copy number, that is, copy number 104, there's another block that says "attachment" or "Annex number 1-12."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This one I think also has some -- well, it's got some ink markings, but -- I believe. You can forget things very quickly in a minute or two -- I believe they're really just marking along in the margin to draw attention to particular paragraphs, rather than words written on. Do you want to have a look and just confirm that -- without dwelling in detail on them that that's basically the position. Somebody has inked quite a number of lines in the margin against particular paragraphs but not written any words that I noticed.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a few words. These are different notations than we've seen in copy number 96, but again, the whole document here is a photocopy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. So -- well, thank you. It's different from 96, but you said there are a few words there somewhere.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And then this is -- the next one has got an extra cover sheet, which may be entirely internal. I simply don't know. But this is also a 96. This doesn't have any of those other numbers, then, the 24, 26, and so on. It just has "96." It doesn't appear -- put it this way -- to add anything to the previous versions of 96 that we've said, but perhaps that's the way I'll put the question, Mr. Treanor. Do you -- if you look at this, does it, in your view, potentially add anything at all, have any significance in addition to the number 96 documents that we've already seen?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't see any handwritten notations in here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Does it -- have you got the other -- I'm not sure whether they're with the Trial Chamber now or with you. Have you got the other 96s, or -- if -- could you -- I wonder if you could just say whether it appears that they are, again, either copies of each other or derived from the same document. And the clue to that is, I'd suggest, the "96" which has been inked in by somebody. Do they look the same?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. I mean, other than the lack of notations, they would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I was talking about the actual numbering, the "96".

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether the number is the same? Whether it appears to be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, whether it appears to be the same. I don't mean whether it's the same number, as opposed to 95 or 97. Whether it appears to be written --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: They're exact copies of each other --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Appears to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Or of some other document.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Appear to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And this -- the next one. We're not far from the end here. The next one has a cover sheet, again, 11/3 -- or it's a Roman II/3, and that's a 104 version. We've seen 104 before. And I'd ask you the same question there, in the same form: Does that appear to -- if you could have a look at that -- Does that appear to potentially add anything of significance, anything different by comparison with the previous number 104 document that we had seen?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: This appears to be the same. Except, of course, it's missing the attachment number --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that was found on the cover page of the first 104.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I've found yet another number 100 in the pile. If I may hand that up. The same question here, Mr. Treanor: Does this document numbered 100, does that appear to add anything of significance, of any material difference, as compared with the previous numbered 100 versions that you've seen today?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't appear to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. And the next one I'm handing up. It looks like number 47 to me, as far as I can see. It's 047. Do you see that, Mr. Treanor?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This has one or two markings that I saw in briefly inspecting it. Not words but simple markings; one of a heading and one against a particular paragraph. But apart from that, in its typeface and its presentation and content, does it appear to you to be exactly the same as several other versions that we've already seen in the last few minutes?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does, except that this appears to be an original numbered copy; that is to say, the number 47 is written in blue ink.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's actual ink.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the notations inside the document are in blue ink.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. Yes. It's a blue -- it's a blue ink, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this document appears to come from the Sarajevo collection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. But so far that's the -- yes, that's right, that's the only one that appears to be an original, in the sense of bearing --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the sense of having blue ink on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: An ink marking, as opposed to something that's pretty obviously a photocopy.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the next one is numbered 93. It comes with its own plastic folder, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we could just put the front sheet on the ELMO again at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Well, you're seeing something which, if anyone else had missed it, the usher was alert and said have you seen it, which is that on the back of this last page of this document are some quite extensive manuscript notes. But let's have the -- I don't think we've had the front sheet. Let's have the front sheet, on the ELMO, the cover sheet first, and then perhaps we might have that back page with the manuscript notes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That copy also appears to come from the Sarajevo collection. The number 93 is a photocopy -- a photocopied number. However, there are original blue-ink notations on the reverse of the last page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. They're quite extensive. We can see that. The -- just -- we won't spend time on it right now, or at least I'm not proposing to spend time on it until people have had a chance to just consider what these are. But could you just tell us what the -- say, the first two say, 93A and 93B. Can you read, first of all, what that says?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of it. It is rather Cyrillic handwriting. It tends to be. 93A, I'm not sure. 93B appears to be Stanisic Mico. 93C appears to be Banja Luka, followed by something else. 93D is Doboj. 93E is Tuzla. 93F --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I won't for the moment ask you to go right through that, Mr. Treanor. We may, of course, have to come back to that.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think 93A is -- might be Stojan Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Does the -- would Your Honours like to see that itself at the moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It very much depends on what importance it gets in the further examination of the witness. Just to see some handwriting, the Chamber has seen some handwriting before, so it very much depends on the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not pressing it on Your Honours at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then the next --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would Your Honour just forgive me one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. May I hand up this. This is also one of four. Perhaps I -- I'll comment in advance, rather than just try to remember it. And then you would be able to confirm or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This one is on that sort of rather chemical old-fashioned fax paper, because we're going back to 1991. And I should say it's probably just as easy, Your Honour, if I indicate what's there and then Mr. Treanor can look at it and everybody else can look at it, for that matter. This does appear to have been faxed by somebody to somebody, because it says across the top in type, "23/12/91, 13/11, Sipad, Komerc, GM, SA," and it is that fax pager that we're familiar with from some years ago, before plain-paper faxes took over in most parts. It appears to be faxed. It's a faint copy. It looks like the original fax and it's a very faint copy it's got a lot of blue ink underlinings and circlings, but I think not writing. It's got some highlighting on it. It's also got some Tipp-Ex on it of some sort at all. And it's got on the front page -- I said it didn't have words, but on the front page it's got some annotation of actual words in manuscript, the ink throughout being blue. So with that description, may I hand that up to you, Mr. Treanor. You'll see, I think, still, you'll be able to see my summary of whey saw on that document on the screen on the transcript. Perhaps you could just indicate briefly whether you agree whether that's an accurate summary of what we actually physically see.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But it doesn't appear to be a complete copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that. Thank you, Mr. Treanor. Could you indicate what is the incompleteness.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There appears to be one or more pages missing from the end of the document. I didn't -- I noticed that when I got to the end, that it wasn't the end. Maybe some of the pages from inside are missing as well. But one or more pages is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it's 104, as I indicated, and we'd seen 104 before.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think we've seen it twice before, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether it's complete or not is a different question, but the stamp numbers do not correspond with the numbers of the pages themselves, so there's at least something ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, then, the last one, I think it is, has got a different form of numbering. It's -- where we've seen 93, 100, 104 and so on -- or 96, perhaps it was -- we see 101, then a hyphen and a 3. But otherwise -- I'd just at this point hand it up to you, please, Mr. Treanor. Could we see the front page. But there is one other very noticeable difference that I suggest to you here. As compared with I think every one of the other documents that we have seen at this run, which is that it is in -- it's in a different typeface with, among other things, the result that the layout is different; it's actually on a -- different number of pages. Is document is shorter. It's simply -- I think it's shorter, rather than longer. It's on a slightly different typeface ad it's on fewer pages. I think it's six, as opposed to ten. Perhaps the precise discrepancy doesn't --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I can compare that with the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course I think that's a fair opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If Mr. Treanor could be given one of the -- I don't think it matters which one, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But identify it for us, so we know which one you're comparing it with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Treanor, may I invite you to take a plain-paper copy, because there were some peculiar aspects on the thermic paper copy. So if you would compare it with one of the many others that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I would certainly -- Mr. Treanor, I'd endorse His Honour's suggestion, with respect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that's the one I wanted to compare it with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No. For the immediate purposes, Mr. Treanor, His Honour is inviting you to take one of the other copies and not the fax copy as your comparator. Just any one would do, yes. As long as we know which one it is, then. So it's the one numbered 100 that has the number 26 chopped off at the top that you referred to earlier.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, just on a quick examination, the whole document appears to be there, but it is indeed a different layout.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: A different format.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: To be specific, it is different typeface, isn't it? Well, have a look, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's certainly set out on the page differently, and therefore the number -- total number of pages is shorter, but -- so it's certainly a different-type copy. Well, not being an expert in typefaces, I would say that it does appear to be different in that the letters in the shorter version appear to be closer together than the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'm only really asking you not because you're an expert -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the Chamber have the last two copies that were in the hands of Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Treanor, I was going to say I'm only asking you not in the first place because you purport to be an expert but because you have the documents at the time. But of course the Trial Chamber can see as well as anybody else.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letters are darker, of course; although sometimes differences between photocopies can account for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Your Honours, since it's the Trial Chamber that now physically has these documents, may I suggest that I think -- this is from recollection that the last document, 101-3, the whole content, although Mr. Treanor has confirmed it's got the same overall content, is then on six pages only, as opposed to I think it's ten -- it's nine or ten on the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I can confirm the six, and the other one is ten. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. What -- oh, well, I don't want to be in contempt of court for retaining a clear plastic folder. Whether it came from Sarajevo or out of the budget of the ICTY, I don't know. But for completeness, it goes with the documents. Your Honour, from a purely practical point of view, it may be actually the simplest thing is simply to have the whole lot copied, rather than spend time debating which ones should be copied. So it's a few minutes' work. I think in this particular instance the invitation goes to others to photocopy it because they, I think, would prefer to keep custody of these documents. Could I ask if the Prosecution could arrange that overnight, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before doing so, could perhaps, please, these two copies be put on the ELMO again. On the page I opened, could we just move a bit upwards. Yes. And could you perhaps try to put at the same time where it says "2" and then I take it that it says Variant B and then another line in capitals, a similar part. Yes, but that's not the same part. On the other -- Mr. Treanor, could you find the relevant part in the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So what follows from number 8 and then to -- where it seems to say "Variant B." If you compare those two parts, Mr. Treanor, would you still think that it's a matter of spacing or are there other differences? Perhaps if you concentrate on the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we can see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- the beginning of paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We can see -- well, we can't see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to move a little bit downwards, the both of them, I think. Yes. I think now -- yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That in the top version the heading "2, Variant B" is underlined in the bottom version. It's not underlined in the top version. It's underlined in the bottom version. And the second heading that comes on the next line, exactly the opposite is the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any other difference in this part, these specific two lines? Perhaps you could concentrate on the B.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe if I could just have a look at them. What -- in the version in which the top heading is not underlined, the letter B is not enclosed in quotation marks; in the version in which that heading is underlined, the letter -- the Cyrillic letter "B" is enclosed in quotation marks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you -- then perhaps -- these were my questions in respect of after having inspected the documents. So if there are no further questions in this respect, Mr. Stewart, you could get your copies back.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'd simply ask the practical question whether the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I'd simply ask the practical question whether the Prosecution would be able to arrange photocopying overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't think that will be a problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It may be, Mr. Treanor, that my next question would require us to come back when we've got these documents. But are you able at the moment, on what you've seen, to cast any light on the variations in the form of the document and, in particular, that variation between the six-page document in the darker and apparently slighter smaller typeface, 101-3, and for practical purposes all the others which are in another typeface, apparently, and takes nine or ten pages?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't have any particular knowledge of a reason for the differences among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Turning now to perhaps a bit more substance, then. The top left cover page, and of course if at any point you require to look at a document, please say so. But we can I think for now we can work for practical purposes from the copy which is at bundle 6, tab 66. And you have the English and, of course; the original B/C/S version. And it probably doesn't matter which one. It's a copy of the one in the bundle. But it's number 100, anyway, isn't it, the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The top left-hand cover page, as we've seen before, refers to the Serbian Democratic Party, I'm reading the English, of course, Bosnia and Herzegovina, SDS Main Board. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Does it say "SDS Main Board" or just simply "Main Board"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says "Serbian Democratic Party of Bosnia and Herzegovina," all in capitals. And then under that in mostly small letters but beginning with a capital -- in the first word, it says "Main Board."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. The -- but I think you've said, but to confirm, there is no record whatever, is there, of this document ever having been -- I don't mean number 100, but you know what I mean when I say "this document." In record whatever of this document ever having been adopted or approved by the Main Board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure what you mean by "a record" in this sense. There are documents which refer to this document, both before and after the 19th of December, but there is no document on the order of, say, the records of the Assembly session at which this document is discussed and adopted by the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, in the case of either a record of any proceedings of the Main Board or a record of any proceedings of the Assembly, we do not see this document ever having been adopted or approved, do we?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: In such a document embodying the proceedings of a session, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you -- your implicit qualification in your answer is that somewhere else we see an indication of such adoption or approval; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- as I indicated before, there are other documents both before and after the 19th of December, 1991 which appear to refer to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So this is the evidence that you've given previously. And it is pretty clear what you're saying. The evidence you've given previously from which you, including your report, from which you draw inferences that it emanated from the main organs of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, what was the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That when you say there are documents before and after the 19th of December which appear to refer to this document, that what you're saying is - and I think what you have already said - is that you draw inferences from other material that this particular document did have its origin with one or other of the main organs of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But there's also the fact that this document on its face indicates that it comes from the Main Board of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it indicates -- you just have in mind that it says "Main Board."

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So it's -- as a sort of Latin tag for it, omnia praesumuntur or something, that you're starting with a presumption that a document has got on it in a typeface that it's from the Main Board that unless somebody -- unless somebody shows me something different, I'm going to take it that it came from the Main Board. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pretty much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At the other end of the document, in the English version it ends up "SDS Crisis Headquarters." Just tell us -- well, tell the Trial Chamber, please, exactly what the B/C/S version of the document says at the end after the last numbered paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would render that as Crisis Staff of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it's in typeface --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all in capital letters --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, apparently -- apparently the same typeface, but in capital letters.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Nobody's manuscript signature?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. There's no signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you aware of any place to start -- sorry, you'll have to give it to me again or I'll just have to check what you said. Yes. Are you -- sorry, forget place. Are you aware of any body or organ that ever bore the title - as it appears in B/C/S, of course, in the version you're looking at - of "Crisis Staff of the SDS"?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are only two documents that I can bring to mind at this point which refer to a Crisis Staff within the context of the SDS. One is a telephone conversation from, I believe, July 1991 in which Dr. Karadzic tells the caller twice, I believe, that "We have a Crisis Staff." The other is a document from early March 1992 which purports to come from an SDS Crisis Staff. I can't remember the exact wording of that title, whether it was the Crisis Staff of the SDS or something else, but it was -- or spelled out the Crisis Staff of the Serbian Democratic Party. I can't remember the exact words. But "Crisis Staff" was part of the name given to the organ that purported to issue that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In your evidence in chief and the transcript reference there is 1509, you had said that it was a body the time and composition of which you did not know.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. That's correct. Those are just two references to such a body, and it's a composition or -- the date of its formation or duration of its activities are not otherwise known to me through the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, I'm coming on to what's really a chapter in -- under this Variant A and B heading. I'm in Your Honour's hands, but it may be that starting a chapter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. We'll continue until 7.00, so -- so if that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I -- sorry, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's quarter to 2.00 in the afternoon to 7.00 in evening, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I got it in my head --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A few chapters, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It was probably just wishful thinking, Your Honour. But the -- I'll press on, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The Assembly had already adopted a recommendation on broadly the same topic, and that's an introduction to a question. We're going to go to -- may I take you to bundle 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If the document could be put on the ELMO. If you could work on that basis, then everyone has it in front of himself. But if, Mr. Treanor, you'd need to look at it more closely, then, of course, you take it off from the ELMO and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps I could look at the B/C/S while the English is on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That could be a good solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, it was 62, tab 62.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you indicate the page, because in English is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's page 2 -- well, in fact, we -- yes, page 2. It's just the front sheet or the cover sheet which is page 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you'd give the whole of the bundle to Mr. Treanor, then he'll find page 2 only in the B/C/S version. If you'd give it to Mr. Treanor, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: On the agenda -- this is towards the bottom of page 2 --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Agenda, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- item 2 is: "Proposed recommendation (decision) on the establishment of Municipal Assemblies of the Serbian People in Bosnia and Herzegovina." So that was the item that was formally on the agenda. And then the discussion starts at page 9 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, what pages are you going to deal with? Because then Madam Usher can take them out all at the same time, instead of one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because now we have to remove it again from Mr. Treanor to the usher and then have to find the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What other pages will you refer to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's also --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Madam Usher took them all out in order to be on the safe time. Okay. We'll now move to page 9, I do understand. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it's -- it's heading number 2, "Proposed recommendation (decision) on the establishment of Municipal Assemblies of the Serbian People." So it reflects that item in the agenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We see Dr. Milanovic: "Please read the proposed recommendation decision," the chairman being Mr. Krajisnik, of course, of this particular meeting. "Recommendation." There's a subheading there. And then it is "groups of deputies." Do you see that paragraph, Mr. Treanor? Because you're in the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You're following it in the B/C/S, are you?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. "Groups of deputies of the Serbian Democratic Party in Municipal Assemblies in Bosnia and Herzegovina in which the Serbian Democratic Party does not have the majority of the seats are recommended to pass decisions on the establishment of Municipal Assemblies of the Serbian People." Now, it's -- would you agree it's correct that if we cross-refer to Variant A and B -- we've got that in English. As I said, it's 6/66 -- that this, not being exactly the same, but this paragraph of the recommendation is very broadly the same as Variant B, first level, paragraph 4? Do you -- have you got Variant A and B somewhere? It's in Volume 6, the first tab, 66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, it's true that it's late in the day. If you --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I realise, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you are not putting off your microphone, then sooner or later your conversations among Defence counsel will, translated, appear on the transcript, if that's the risk you are taking. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At least it wasn't the worst that could happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Looking at first level, paragraph 4, very broadly is it covering the same ground?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to remind myself. We're under Roman II, Variant B?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, we are. Yes. I beg your pardon. It's page 5 of the English version of the document. That's right. We're under Roman II, Variant B, first level.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: First level.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are they approximately the same, is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Broadly they're the same. There are some differences. Would you like me -- would you like me to go into them?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, the differences -- actually, the differences are not obscure, are they -- well, Mr. Treanor, yes. You're the witness. You're the expert. You just identify the differences for us.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, to cut to the chase, the document adopted by the Assembly, as I think I indicated in my testimony, is a recommendation, and it's a recommendation to the clubs of assemblymen of the Serbian Democratic Party in particular municipalities, and it calls on them to do something, that is, found an Assembly of the Serbian People. In the Variant A and B document, it isn't quite clear who the instruction is addressed to since it's couched in the infinitive, but it basically says that an Assembly of the Serbian People should be formed from the assemblymen, from the ranks of the Serbian people, in particular municipalities and presidents of the local; that is, the local community within the municipality -- within the municipalities, the local community boards of the SDS. So the composition is a little bit different here, and the actors are described a little bit differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Where you referred a moment ago to "an Assembly of the Serbian People being formed from the assemblymen from the ranks of the Serbian people," where are you getting the ranks of the Serbian people from? You're looking at the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. This is in the Variant A and B document you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. But are you looking at Variant A or Variant B at the moment?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got to double-check here. Variant B.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: Variant B, first degree, paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you referring to, Mr. Stewart, to where the witness told us about the clubs of assemblymen to whom it was addressed? Is that the part you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No. It was -- Your Honour, it was where the witness said -- it isn't quite clear, but line 16 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At line 15: "It isn't quite clear who the instruction is addressed to since it's couched in the infinitive, but it basically says that an Assembly of the Serbian People should be formed from the assemblymen, from the ranks of the Serbian People in particular municipalities..." And I was just slightly puzzled, Mr. Treanor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Are you getting that from -- the reference to the ranks of the Serbian people in particular municipalities, is that coming specifically from the text?

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I left out a word. From the ranks of the Serbian people in the Assembly of the Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Oh. Yes, that was --

utterances.speaker: PATRICK TREANOR [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, that was what threw me, there -- Mr. Treanor. It was just, of course, I'm working from the English translation, but I was having difficulty matching that with what you could have got from the B/C/S. Yes, I see. That clarifies that point. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, it's now close to 7.00. I don't know whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- your wishes have changed or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, it's fairly late in the day, Your Honour, after all, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm in the Tribunal's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you'd find a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's as suitable a moment as any, if that would be convenient for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd first like to ask Madam Usher to escort the witness out of the courtroom, but not after, Mr. Treanor, I've instructed you again not to speak with anyone about the testimony already given and still to be given in this court. And we'll sit tomorrow at 9.00, this same courtroom, so we expect you then back, if possible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we adjourn, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tomorrow we'll get copies of all the different versions of this document. Will there be any substantial issue, then, on all these versions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I don't think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because if it was your intention to establish that there were different versions and just present different versions to us, I don't know whether there's anything more on your mind to say, "Well, we have handwritten versions. We have six-page versions. We have fax versions. We have --" Is there anything else we'll hear about these versions by tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I doubt it, Your Honour, for this reason: I think having tested the ground by one or two questions to Mr. Treanor, it seems apparent that he personally hasn't got really any significant light to cast on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the first thing, of course, was to establish that there are some different versions. That took us some 50 minutes. And if it would have been efficiently, ten minutes would have been good enough. You could have indicated to the witness that we have five copies with the number 100 on it, although with different stamps on it, and then give it to him and say would you agree with me that we have versions with handwriting on it and copied versions of that, handwritten versions, and then it would have taken us ten minutes, certainly not more, to establish that we have these 12 or 13 or 14, how many, and then of course you could have asked him whether he has any explanation than go into any details. But to spend 45 minutes just to hear from him that he has no explanation for the differences is not a very efficient way of examining a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: With the greatest respect, Your Honour, I disagree. The -- it's only at the end of such cross-examination it's possible to look back and see what its value and usefulness has been. It is absolutely essential in relation to such important documents that I should have explored with Mr. Treanor the details of those documents in relation to the numbering, the format, and all those details in order to be absolutely satisfied that they are not of any significance. And it is only by doing a thorough cross-examination in that way that it is possible to reach that conclusion. It is then of course extremely easy to look back and say, "Well, since that is all we have got from it, it could have been got in five minutes." But in fact, with the greatest respect, Your Honour, it could not. And that's the point of such a cross-examination. I didn't wish to spend any longer on those documents than I did. But I did wish to be absolutely satisfied that if there was no significance in discrepancies among these documents, that was clear. The only point which remains now in effect, because it seems unlikely that Mr. Treanor can cast any light, because at the end of the cross-examination in order to avoid us spending unnecessary time overnight and in order to be as clear as we could where we were going tomorrow, I did ask him that question. But there does remain the issue of the manuscript annotations on those documents, which also have to be considered before we can see where we're going. But of course, I do naturally pay the greatest respect to guidance and even rebuke by the Tribunal. But I will say with the greatest respect, Your Honour, I do not believe that inappropriate time was spent on that aspect of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not going to respond to it at this very moment. We'll first adjourn until tomorrow morning. If there's anything more to be said about it, I'll do that. If not, we'll leave it to this. We adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.00, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 16th day of April, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.04 p.m.,
